title: Austempering Temperature and Isothermal-Holding Effects on the Microstructure and Mechanical–Tribological Response of Si–Mo Alloyed Ferritic Ductile Iron Produced by SSF
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the influence of austempering temperature and isothermal-holding time on the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and tribological performance of Si–Mo alloyed ferritic ductile iron produced by the solution-strengthened foundry (SSF) route. After austenitization at 900 °C for 90 min, the specimens were salt bath austempered at 300, 350, and 400 °C for 30 and 90 min. The results showed that the austempering parameters influenced the evolution of the ausferritic matrix, retained austenite characteristics, and the resulting mechanical and tribological response. Among the investigated conditions, the specimen austempered at 300 °C for 30 min exhibited the highest ultimate tensile strength (1344.8 MPa ± 32.97) and hardness (52.92 HRC ± 1.64), as well as the lowest specific wear rate. The specimen austempered at 300 °C for 90 min showed the highest impact energy (54.7 J ± 4.443). These findings indicate that lower austempering temperatures favor a finer ausferritic structure, resulting in improved strength and wear resistance, whereas longer holding at the same temperature is more favorable for impact toughness. SEM examination showed that abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear mechanisms were present depending on the matrix condition. Overall, the study demonstrates that austempering parameters play a critical role in controlling microstructural evolution and the resulting mechanical–tribological performance.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Damage mechanisms are among the most critical factors influencing machine design, as failures associated with fracture, wear, and surface degradation can result in substantial economic losses. 1  Over the past five decades, austempered ductile cast irons (A-DCI) have attracted increasing attention due to their extensive use in machine parts, including sliding components, guide systems, railway equipment, and various mechanical bearings. Their growing adoption in recent years, particularly in automotive applications such as crankshafts, camshafts, and gear components, has been widely documented. 2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5  This prominent interest mainly stems from the balanced set of mechanical properties characteristic of A-DCI, such as elevated yield and tensile strengths, high ductility, 6 , 7  superior toughness, improved wear resistance, reliable fatigue performance, and strong design versatility. 8  Owing to these advantages, A-DCI provides a viable replacement for traditional steel castings, manganese steels, forged components, and even aluminum-based parts. 9 , 10  Another important reason for the industrial preference for ductile irons is their ability to enable the economical production of large, geometrically complex components. 11  Compared with forged steels, ductile irons generally offer cost benefits, especially when used in place of heat-treatable steels or cast steels. 12 ,  13 – 14  However, while these studies primarily focus on conventional ADI systems, the present study specifically addresses the behavior of Si–Mo alloyed ferritic ductile iron subjected to austempering. Therefore, a clear transition from general ADI knowledge to the specific material system investigated here is required.

Because many engineering applications of austempered ductile iron (ADI) demand excellent durability, dimensional stability, and high reliability, these materials have attained a notable position in the manufacturing sector. 12  The enhanced performance of ductile iron originates from its characteristic microstructure composed of graphite nodules embedded within a matrix of ferrite, bainite, or pearlite phases. 10 , 15  In the case of ADI, the microstructure consists of ausferrite, which is formed by an acicular ferrite phase intermixed with carbon-enriched retained austenite and surrounded by nodular graphite particles. 16  The formation of this ausferritic structure occurs through a two-stage transformation mechanism during austempering: Stage I involves the transformation of austenite into ausferrite with carbon partitioning into the remaining austenite, whereas Stage II is associated with the decomposition of retained austenite into ferrite and carbides if the process is prolonged. 17  Therefore, controlling the extent of Stage I while suppressing Stage II is critical for achieving an optimal balance between strength and ductility.

As established in the literature, adjustments to heat-treatment paths, along with the effects of alloying constituents, are widely used to modify the microstructure and the resulting mechanical behavior of ductile irons. 10  In particular, silicon plays a key role in suppressing carbide formation and promoting ferritic matrices. At the same time, molybdenum can influence hardenability and transformation kinetics. Still, it may also increase the tendency for carbide precipitation under certain conditions. Additionally, copper is known to stabilize austenite and enhance hardenability, thereby affecting the kinetics of ausferrite formation and the resulting mechanical properties. 14  For austempered ductile irons, the ausferritic phase is produced through a multi-stage thermal treatment. The process typically includes austenitizing within the 700–1000 °C temperature window, followed by transferring the material to a salt bath maintained at 250–450 °C, where subsequent austempering occurs at controlled holding times. 16 , 18

In this study, the material investigated is a Si–Mo alloyed solution-strengthened ferritic ductile iron rather than a conventional ADI system. Unlike traditional ADI alloys, which are typically based on pearlitic or mixed matrices, the present material has a predominantly ferritic matrix and elevated Si and Mo contents, which significantly influence transformation kinetics and carbon partitioning during austempering. Therefore, the response to austempering may differ significantly due to its initial ferritic matrix and alloy chemistry. This research focuses on enhancing the mechanical performance of high-silicon Si–Mo ductile iron by applying austempering treatments under controlled temperature and time conditions. To assess the material’s response in various regions of the casting, dedicated specimens were extracted from specific locations of the produced sample, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation.

Although several studies have investigated austempering behavior in ductile irons with varying alloying additions, the combined effects of low-temperature and short-duration austempering schedules in Si–Mo alloyed ferritic ductile irons have not been systematically examined within a unified experimental framework. 14 , 17  Previous studies are generally limited to conventional ADI compositions and relatively narrow processing windows, often focusing on either temperature or holding time in isolation rather than on their combined influence. Existing studies often focus on limited parameter ranges or specific property sets, making it difficult to establish comprehensive relationships between processing conditions and performance. Moreover, while prior research has addressed mechanical or tribological properties individually, integrated evaluations considering both aspects simultaneously remain relatively limited and context-dependent. 14 , 17  Therefore, the primary objective of this study is to investigate the influence of austempering temperature and holding time on the microstructural evolution, mechanical properties, and frictional behavior of Si–Mo alloyed ferritic ductile iron, with particular emphasis on establishing correlations between processing parameters and overall material performance.

sections.heading: Material Preparation and Heat Treatment
paragraphs: The ductile cast iron with spheroidal graphite (DCI) was produced by melting the charge materials in a 300 kg induction furnace operating at 1510 °C ± 10 °C. The charge consisted of ductile iron returns, steel scrap, and ductile iron scrap. To tailor the transformation behavior during subsequent heat treatment, molybdenum (0.40 wt.%) was deliberately added in the form of ferromolybdenum (Fe–Mo) to enhance hardenability and promote the formation of a refined ausferritic microstructure.

For spheroidization, the molten metal was transferred into a sandwich-type treatment ladle containing a Mg-bearing Fe–Si alloy (Fe–Si–Mg, ~5–6 wt.% Mg). Following this treatment, a commercial ferrosilicon-based inoculant (Fe–75Si with Ba and Ca additions) was introduced at approximately 0.2–0.3 wt.% as a post-inoculant to promote graphite nucleation and stabilize nodule formation. This sequential spheroidization and inoculation strategy was employed to ensure a uniform and well-developed nodular graphite morphology.

The molten metal was subsequently cast into Y-shaped molds (25 mm thickness) prepared using a dry-sand molding process in accordance with ASTM A781. 1  The melt was transferred to the pouring ladle at approximately 1445 °C ± 15 °C and then poured into the molds. Accordingly, all melting, treatment, and casting stages were carried out under controlled conditions to ensure process reproducibility and minimize variability in the resulting microstructure.

The elemental chemical composition of the produced cast iron, consisting of spheroidal graphite embedded in a ferritic matrix, is presented in Table  1 . Although the experimental composition is compared with ASTM A586-84 in Table  1 , the alloy was intentionally designed as a modified composition rather than a strictly standard-compliant grade. In particular, the elevated Cu (0.80 wt.%) and Mo (0.40 wt.%) contents were purposefully selected to investigate their combined influence on hardenability, transformation kinetics, and the resulting austempering response. Therefore, ASTM A586-84 was used only as a reference framework for comparison. The chemical composition was determined in the as-cast condition using optical emission spectroscopy (OES) for metallic elements 19 , 20  and combustion analysis for carbon and sulfur contents, in accordance with ASTM E351-18 and ASTM E1019-18 standards. 21 , 22  Performing the analysis prior to heat treatment ensured that the alloy’s baseline composition was accurately established, without any influence from thermal processing.

In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was employed for microstructural characterization and qualitative/local verification of elemental distribution within the matrix and graphite nodules, as shown in Figure  1 . This combined SEM–EDS analysis provided complementary insight into both morphological features and localized compositional variations within the cast structure. Figure 1 SEM microstructure and corresponding EDS results used for qualitative/local verification of elemental distribution in the produced ductile cast iron (DCI).

To obtain the austempered microstructure in the ductile iron specimens, the material was austenitized at 900 °C for 90 min and then immediately transferred to a temperature-controlled salt bath containing Petrofer AS 135 heat-treatment salt, composed of equal proportions of NaNO 3  and KNO 3 . This two-step thermal treatment was designed to promote controlled ausferritic transformation under isothermal conditions. The transfer time between removal from the furnace and immersion in the salt bath was kept below 5 s for all specimens in order to minimize uncontrolled cooling and suppress the formation of unintended transformation products prior to the isothermal stage.

During the austempering stage, each specimen was held isothermally at 300 °C, 350 °C, and 400 °C for 30 min and 90 min as separate experimental conditions. After the isothermal-holding step, the specimens were allowed to cool naturally to room temperature, thereby completing the austempering cycle, as shown in Figure  2 . Here, natural cooling refers to still-air cooling under laboratory ambient conditions without the application of any external cooling medium or forced quenching. Figure 2 Overview of the heat-treatment steps applied to the experimental specimens.

Because uncontrolled final cooling may promote partial transformation of metastable blocky austenite, particularly below the Ms temperature, this possibility was taken into account when interpreting the hardness and tensile results. However, no clear microstructural evidence indicating significant martensite formation was observed in SEM examinations or XRD patterns of the investigated specimens. In addition, the selected austempering temperatures and holding times were determined based on previous studies of austempered ductile irons and alloy-modified ductile iron systems to represent lower, intermediate, and upper ausferritic transformation conditions within a consistent experimental framework.

To facilitate clear and consistent identification of the ductile cast iron specimens throughout the graphs and figures, the produced and heat-treated samples were re-designated using the customized labels given in Table  2 . All specimens used for microstructural and mechanical characterization were extracted from the same representative section of the Y-block casting in order to minimize variations associated with local cooling-rate differences. In addition, sampling was performed from equivalent locations relative to the riser and mold geometry to maintain segregation- and solidification-related effects as consistent as possible among all specimens. sections.heading: Microstructural Analysis
paragraphs: The microstructural characterization of the specimens was performed using a LISS XJL-17X optical microscope (OM), a FEI QUANTA FEG 250 scanning electron microscope (SEM), a BRUKER D8 ADVANCE TWIN-TWIN X-ray diffractometer (XRD), and an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) system. All sample preparation procedures were conducted in strict accordance with the metallographic guidelines specified in ASTM E3-11, 23  ensuring consistency and reproducibility of the obtained results. In these examinations, tensile specimens extracted from Y-block castings were used as representative regions.

In Equations  1  and  2 , Vγ and Vα′ represent the volume fractions of the γ (austenite) and α′ (ferrite) phases, respectively, while Iγ and Iα′ correspond to the relative integrated intensities of the γ(111) and α(110) diffraction peaks obtained from XRD patterns. These intensity values were determined through image processing and peak analysis performed in Python using the NumPy and SciPy libraries, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reproducibility of the calculations. Equation  3  defines Cγ as the carbon content of the austenitic phase, where aγ denotes the lattice parameter of γ-iron. This relation is based on the well-established lattice parameter–carbon content correlation widely used for retained austenite evaluation in ferrous systems. 4 , 25 , 26

sections.heading: Tensile–Hardness and Impact Testing
paragraphs: To evaluate the influence of microstructural variations induced by different salt-bath austempering temperatures and holding times on material behavior, tensile, hardness, and Charpy impact tests were conducted on the prepared specimens. This combined approach enabled a comprehensive assessment of strength, ductility, and toughness characteristics under varying processing conditions.

Cylindrical tensile specimens with a diameter of 6 mm and a gauge length of 30 mm were machined from Y-block castings in accordance with ASTM E8M standards. Tensile tests were performed using a 50 kN UTEST universal testing machine at a constant crosshead speed of 2 mm/min. An extensometer was attached to the gauge length to ensure precise measurement of yield strength and elongation, thereby improving the accuracy of deformation-related parameters. For each condition, five tensile tests were conducted to ensure statistical reliability.

For impact testing, specimens with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm containing a standard V-notch were prepared in accordance with ASTM A897 and ASTM E23 standards. All specimens were carefully machined to maintain consistent notch geometry, which is critical for ensuring comparability of impact energy results. The Charpy impact tests were carried out using a Mohr & Federhaff PSW 30/15 testing machine with a maximum capacity of 300 J. To minimize experimental variability and improve data reliability, five independent measurements were performed for each condition at ambient temperature (20 °C ± 5 °C), and the average values were reported.

Hardness measurements were performed using the Rockwell C scale (150 kgf load) on a TIME 6102DT desktop hardness tester. For each austempered condition, five measurements were taken at different locations on the specimen surface to account for possible local heterogeneities. The reported hardness values represent the arithmetic mean of these measurements.

sections.heading: Tribological Performance (Abrasive Wear Test)
paragraphs: To evaluate the tribological behavior of the test specimens, including mass loss, specific wear rate, and coefficient of friction, a fixed-abrasive block-on-disk wear test system was employed. This method was selected to provide a controlled comparison of wear resistance under identical abrasive and loading conditions. The abrasive disk used in the experiments was prepared by mounting SiC sandpaper onto a metallic disk. The wear behavior of specimens with dimensions 10 × 10 × 15 mm was examined under dry sliding conditions using 150-mesh abrasive sandpaper and three normal loads of 20 N, 40 N, and 60 N. The sliding speed was maintained at 0.5 m/s, and the test duration was fixed at 100 s. The density (ρ) of the ductile cast iron specimens was measured using the Archimedes principle, and an average value of 7.11 g/cm 3  was used for all calculations.

These parameters were kept constant throughout the experiments to ensure that the observed differences in wear behavior could be directly associated with the microstructural variations induced by the heat-treatment conditions. For each wear condition, three independent tests were performed on each specimen.

Following the wear tests, the worn surfaces were examined using optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to identify the dominant surface damage features and wear mechanisms. This post-test characterization provided direct microstructural evidence for interpreting the quantitative wear results. Weight-loss measurements were carried out before and after each test using a RADWAG precision balance with a sensitivity of 0.01 mg. To improve measurement reliability, each weight-loss determination was repeated five times for every specimen, and the corresponding values were used in the wear-rate calculations.

In this equation, Δw represents the weight loss, ρ is the density of the test specimen, S denotes the sliding distance, and P corresponds to the applied load. This formulation enabled a normalized comparison of wear behavior by accounting for both material density and test severity.

sections.heading: Assessment of Microstructure Analysis
paragraphs: The carbon equivalent, a critical parameter for ductile iron casting properties, was calculated from the percentage-based chemical composition values of the produced samples presented in Table  1 . It was found to fall within the ASTM A536-84 standard ranges. 28  The CE (carbon equivalent) value of the produced ductile iron, calculated using the equation provided below, was determined to be 4.48%, indicating a hypereutectic composition. 29 , 30  This hypereutectic nature suggests a strong tendency for graphite formation during solidification, which is consistent with the observed nodular graphite morphology discussed in subsequent sections.

The phosphorus (P) content in the composition, which is lower than ASTM standards, does not negatively affect the graphite properties, as evidenced by the SEM and optical images presented in Figure  3 . The chromium content is known to promote metastable eutectic transformation and may contribute to the formation of eutectic structures that potentially contain carbides. However, in the present study, no direct experimental evidence (e.g., SEM-EDS carbide identification, XRD carbide peak analysis, or microhardness mapping) was obtained to confirm the presence of carbide phases. Accordingly, the role of chromium is interpreted cautiously as a potential metallurgical influence rather than a confirmed microstructural constituent. Although the ASTM composition standards for ductile iron do not include molybdenum (Mo), the presence of 0.40% Mo in ductile iron not only increases hardenability but also significantly affects transformation kinetics, segregation tendency, and local phase evolution in Si–Mo systems. In particular, Mo segregation in interdendritic regions may locally retard transformation kinetics and promote microstructural heterogeneity, thereby influencing subsequent ausferritic transformation during austempering. Furthermore, depending on the thermal cycle and local chemistry, Mo may also contribute to carbide precipitation. Therefore, the strengthening effect of Mo should not be attributed solely to its interaction with carbon atoms, but also to its influence on diffusion behavior, transformation kinetics, and possible secondary phase formation during austempering. 32  Based on these compositional considerations, the microstructural characterization was systematically evaluated for both as-cast and austempered conditions. Quantitative data on the microstructural characterization of the experimental specimens are presented in Table  3 . Figure 3 Optical (100×) and SEM micrographs of as-cast (DCI) and austempered ductile iron specimens (T1-300, T2-300, T2-400) showing graphite morphology and matrix evolution under different heat-treatment conditions. Table 3 Quantitative Microstructural Parameters of the Experimental Specimens Specimen Nodularity Ratio (%) Nodule Density (nodules/mm 2 ) DCI 88.56 ± 1.97 191.25 ± 24.7 A-900 89.7 ± 2.01 196.08 ± 19.3 T1-300 92.4 ± 3.07 219.61 ± 20.1 T2-300 91.55 ± 3.6 220.78 ± 18.7 T1-350 90.63 ± 3.05 208.49 ± 15.2 T2-350 89.46 ± 3.45 198.01 ± 17.0 T1-400 86.9 ± 4.80 195.42 ± 17.8 T2-400 84.55 ± 5.40 190.64 ± 20.3

Among the experimental samples, the DCI specimens exhibited a nodular density of 191.25 ± 24.7 nodules/mm 2  and a nodularity ratio of 88.56 ± 1.97%, whereas the highest values were calculated for the austempered T2-300 samples. At first glance, the slight increase in nodule density in certain austempered specimens may suggest microstructural refinement; however, this interpretation would be misleading. The slightly higher nodule density observed in certain austempered specimens (e.g., T2-300) should not be attributed to the heat treatment. Graphite nodule count is primarily governed by melt chemistry, inoculation efficiency, and solidification conditions. Therefore, the variations observed after heat treatment are statistically driven rather than physically induced by austempering. These T2-300 samples demonstrated a nodular density of 220.78 ± 18.7 nodules/mm 2  and a nodularity ratio of 92.04 ± 3.07%. For all investigated conditions, the measured graphite nodule count ranged from 190 to 240 nodules/mm 2 , consistent with values reported in the literature for 25 mm Y-block ductile iron castings produced under comparable processing conditions. 31 , 33 , 34  Similarly, the measured nodularity ratios (84.55–92.40%) remain within the expected range for this casting section. These results confirm that austempering does not alter graphite morphology but primarily affects the matrix transformation behavior. Furthermore, although no formal statistical hypothesis test (e.g., t-test) was performed, the observed variations fall within the expected scatter band for specimens extracted from equivalent regions of the same Y-block casting.

In the present study, optical microscope and SEM images of both the austempered and untreated ductile iron samples are presented in Figure  3 . Within this scope, Figure  3  shows microstructural images of the T1-300 sample, which exhibited the highest nodularity ratio; the untreated as-cast ductile iron sample; and the T2-400 sample, which had the lowest nodularity ratio. This selection enables a representative comparison across extreme and intermediate conditions. To illustrate the effect of different austempering durations on the microstructure, comparative microstructural images of T1-300 and T2-300 specimens are presented. Both specimens exhibit similar nodularity ratios (91.55–92.4%) and nodule densities (219.61–220.78 nodules/mm 2 ). As expected, the austempering treatment did not affect the morphology and distribution of graphite nodules. However, differences in the ausferrite content, blocky austenite fraction, and phase distribution were observed in the matrix microstructure as a function of austempering duration and temperature. Thus, the primary microstructural evolution induced by austempering is associated with matrix phase transformation rather than graphite modification.

In the present study, optical microscope and SEM images of both the austempered and untreated ductile iron samples are presented in Figure  3 . Within this scope, Figure  3  shows microstructural images of the T1-300 sample, which exhibited the highest nodularity ratio; the untreated as-cast ductile iron sample; and the T2-400 sample, which had the lowest nodularity ratio. To illustrate the effect of different austempering durations on the microstructure, comparative microstructural images of T1-300 and T2-300 specimens are presented. Both specimens exhibit similar nodularity ratios (91.55-92.4%) and nodule densities (219.61- 220.78 nodules/mm 2 ). As expected, the austempering treatment did not affect the morphology and distribution of graphite nodules. However, differences in the ausferrite content, blocky austenite fraction, and phase distribution were observed in the matrix microstructure as a function of austempering duration and temperature. Thus, the primary microstructural evolution induced by austempering is associated with matrix phase transformation rather than graphite modification.

The observed minor variations in nodularity ratio and nodule count among different heat-treated specimens are therefore attributed to statistical dispersion inherent to image analysis, slight compositional heterogeneity within the casting section, and local microstructural sampling differences rather than to the direct effect of austempering temperature. The heat treatment primarily modifies the matrix phase transformation while preserving the original graphite morphology. This observation reinforces the validity of comparing matrix phases independently of graphite-related parameters. In these images, blocky retained austenite is indicated by yellow arrows, feather-like ausferrite by blue arrows, ferrite by red arrows, and graphite nodules by green arrows. These microstructural findings are consistent with previous studies. 10 , 26 , 35  Furthermore, SEM examination revealed that, in addition to spheroidal morphology, graphite nodules were also present in oval and lamellar forms within the microstructure. Additionally, to identify the phases present in the microstructures of both the as-cast ductile iron sample and the austempered ductile irons, XRD pattern analysis, including peak intensity and peak broadening, was performed. The test specimens were scanned within the 2θ range of 30° to 110° at a scan rate of 0.02°/step. The phase identification results obtained from the XRD analysis of the experimental specimens are shown in Figure  4 . Upon examining the XRD data, it was observed that the microstructures contained not only austenitic phases with characteristic peaks at (111), (200), and (220), but also ferritic/martensitic phases with peaks at (110), (200), and (211). However, it should be emphasized that peak overlap between ferrite and martensite limits definitive phase discrimination when relying solely on peak positions. Therefore, the presence of martensite cannot be conclusively confirmed or excluded within the scope of the present XRD analysis, and the phase interpretation should be considered with caution. For this reason, subsequent phase quantification is discussed in a comparative framework rather than as absolute phase identification. Figure 4 XRD pattern of the experimental specimens.

According to the XRD results shown in Figure  4 , increases in both austempering temperature and holding time resulted in a clear increase in the intensity of diffraction peaks associated with retained austenite. Using the established XRD-based quantitative phase analysis equations (Eqs.  1 – 3 ), the retained austenite volume fraction (Vγ) and the austenitic carbon content (Cγ) were calculated from the relative peak intensities and the γ lattice parameter, respectively. The resulting quantitative values are presented in Figure  5 . The amount of retained austenite was found to be influenced by both the austempering temperature and the isothermal-holding time. Specifically, higher temperatures and longer durations promoted the stabilization of retained austenite through enhanced carbon partitioning kinetics. Figure 5 Evolution of retained austenite volume fraction (A) and austenitic carbon content (B) with respect to holding time (T1-30 min/T2-90 min) during austempering of ductile cast iron at 300, 350, and 400 °C.

It is well established that during austempering, ausferritic ferrite (α) precipitates from carbon-enriched austenite (γ), while the rejected carbon diffuses into the remaining untransformed austenite, leading to its stabilization. 35 , 36  This partitioning mechanism governs the enrichment and stabilization of retained austenite. As shown in Figure  5 -(A), the retained austenite volume fraction increases progressively with increasing austempering temperature for both holding times. At elevated temperatures (350–400 °C), the driving force for ausferritic transformation decreases, resulting in a larger fraction of untransformed austenite and consequently higher Vγ values. 37 ,  38 – 39  Longer holding durations (90 min) further promote carbon redistribution and phase stabilization, resulting in consistently higher Vγ than 30 min treatments. In contrast, Figure  5 -(B) demonstrates that the carbon concentration within retained austenite (Cγ) decreases with increasing austempering temperature.

The phase fractions and lattice parameters obtained from the Rietveld refinement are summarized in Table  4 . The results indicate that the FCC phase fraction, corresponding to retained austenite, increased with increasing austempering temperature, whereas the BCC phase fraction decreased accordingly. In addition, the refined lattice parameters showed slight variations among the specimens, which may be associated with differences in the carbon enrichment of retained austenite. The refinement quality indicators (χ 2  and Rwp) were within acceptable limits for all specimens, indicating good agreement between the experimental and calculated patterns and supporting the reliability of the phase quantification. Representative refinement results for the T1 series are presented in Figure  6  to illustrate the fitting quality and the temperature-dependent phase evolution in a clear, uncluttered manner. Since the T1 specimens were sufficient to show the variation in the relative contributions of the BCC and FCC phases with austempering temperature, only these patterns were included in the figure for visual clarity. In contrast, the refinement results for both T1 and T2 specimens are provided in Table  4  to provide a complete quantitative dataset and allow direct comparison between the two specimen groups. The XRD patterns were analyzed using full-pattern Rietveld refinement, which enables simultaneous fitting of the entire diffraction profile and reduces uncertainty due to peak overlap and instrumental broadening. In the refinement procedure, pseudo-Voigt peak profiles and background fitting were used to accurately represent the diffraction peaks. As shown in Figure  6 , the refinement was carried out by considering both the BCC (Im-3m) and FCC (Fm-3m) phases. The calculated patterns closely matched the experimental data over the entire measured 2θ range. At the same time, the residual-difference curves remained at low intensity, confirming the robustness of the refinement procedure for phase analysis and retained austenite quantification. Figure 6 Representative Rietveld refinement results of XRD patterns for selected specimens: (A) T1-300, (B) T1-350, (C) T1-400, and (D) DCI. The observed diffraction data (black dots), calculated profiles (red solid lines), and difference curves (gray bottom lines) are presented together with Bragg reflection positions corresponding to BCC (Im-3m) and FCC (Fm-3m) phases.

Consequently, the decreasing Cγ value does not reflect a reduction in total carbon content, but rather a decrease in the average carbon concentration as the austenite volume increases. Furthermore, it is considered that the austenite with fine film morphology formed at lower temperatures is more carbon-enriched. In contrast, the predominance of coarser, blocky morphology austenite at higher temperatures contributes to a reduction in Cγ values. 35 , 37 , 40 , 41  Thus, the combined interpretation of Figures  5 ,  6 , and Table  4  provides a coherent description of the transformation from carbon-rich film-like austenite to less enriched blocky austenite with increasing temperature. Among the austempered specimens, the highest carbon content in the austenite phase was measured as 2.03% ± 0.06 in the specimen held at 300 °C for 90 minutes.

sections.heading: Tensile and Hardness Tests
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows the UTS values for only the specimens exhibiting the highest tensile performance among the investigated conditions. This figure clearly shows that the T1-300 specimen achieved the maximum tensile strength, indicating that low-temperature austempering for a short holding time provides the most favorable condition for strength development. The obtained strength level (~1345 MPa) falls within the upper range reported for austempered ductile iron systems processed at low temperatures, where refined ausferritic microstructures are dominant. This result is mainly associated with the formation of a refined ausferritic microstructure; however, the possible contribution of localized martensitic regions due to incomplete transformation cannot be fully excluded. Therefore, the superior tensile response of T1-300 should be interpreted with caution, as it may result from both microstructural refinement and possible localized hard transformation products. Figure 7 The highest ultimate tensile strength values of spheroidal graphite cast iron materials under different treatment conditions.

Table  5  summarizes the mean ± standard deviation values of UTS, yield strength, elongation, and hardness for all specimens. The data demonstrate that austempering significantly improved both strength and hardness compared with the as-cast DCI condition, confirming the strengthening effect of the ausferritic transformation. At the same time, the elongation values reveal a clear strength–ductility trade-off, especially at lower austempering temperatures where strength and hardness increase while elongation decreases. Among all specimens, T1-300 exhibited the highest UTS and hardness, whereas T2-400 showed the highest elongation, indicating that the mechanical response is highly sensitive to austempering parameters. Figure  8  presents the general variation in tensile strength and hardness for all specimens produced at different austempering temperatures and times. A detailed evaluation of Figure  8 -A shows that austempered specimens exhibit substantially higher tensile strength than the as-cast counterparts. This improvement is attributed to the transformation of the conventional ferritic–pearlitic matrix into an ausferritic structure, which exhibits superior load-bearing capability. When the effect of austempering temperature is considered, the specimens treated at 400°C exhibited the lowest tensile strength values in both time groups, although they showed comparatively higher elongation. This behavior is related to the increasing dominance of ferritic features, the development of coarser feather-like ausferrite, and especially the higher retained austenite fraction at elevated austempering temperatures. 42 ,  43 – 44  In contrast, the highest tensile strength was obtained in the T1-300 specimen, which is consistent with the strengthening effect of a finer ausferritic structure 43 ,  44 ,  45 – 46  (Figure  8 -A). Figure 8 Tensile strength and hardness values of ductile cast iron materials subjected to different treatments.

Figure  8 -(B) shows that hardness follows a trend similar to tensile strength. The hardness values decrease progressively with increasing austempering temperature, confirming that microstructural coarsening reduces resistance to localized plastic deformation. In addition, specimens austempered for 30 minutes showed higher hardness than those austempered for 90 minutes, indicating that prolonged holding promotes ferrite plate coarsening despite retained austenite stabilization. 36 , 47  These findings are fully consistent with previous reports showing that lower austempering temperatures and shorter holding times favor a harder and more refined ausferritic matrix. 38 , 43 , 48 , 50  Moreover, all austempered samples exhibited markedly higher hardness than the as-cast specimens, which also agrees with the findings of Ramos et al. 26  (Figure  8 -B).

sections.heading: Charpy Impact Tests and Fractographic Analysis
paragraphs: Figure  9  presents the Charpy impact energy values obtained from five repeated measurements for each specimen. The results clearly show that the impact performance of the SGCI specimens was strongly influenced by the microstructural changes introduced by the applied heat treatments. Compared with both the as-cast and austenitized conditions, the austempered specimens exhibited markedly improved impact toughness, confirming the beneficial effect of austempering reported in previous studies. 35 , 38  The as-cast sample (DCI) exhibited a moderate impact energy of 23.6 J ±3.165. In contrast, the austenitized sample (A-900) showed the lowest value, 14.5 J ± 2.51, which can be attributed to the formation of a comparatively brittle matrix upon cooling. In contrast, the highest impact energy, 54.7 J ±4.443, was obtained for the T2-300 specimen, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 132% relative to the as-cast condition. This remarkable increase is mainly associated with the ausferritic microstructure, consisting of acicular ferrite and high-carbon retained austenite, together with the enhanced energy absorption capability provided by the mechanical stability of retained austenite through the TRIP effect. 35 , 51  In addition, previous work has shown that higher silicon contents, particularly in the range of 2.4% to 2.8%, may further improve the impact resistance of austempered cast irons 52  (Figure  9 ). Figure 9 Fracture energy values of DCI materials subjected to different treatments.

Figure  9  also demonstrates the strong effect of austempering temperature on impact behavior. Specimens austempered at 300°C and 350°C exhibited higher impact energies because these conditions promoted the formation of a fine ausferritic microstructure composed of thin acicular ferrite and carbon-enriched retained austenite. By contrast, the specimens austempered at 400°C showed a clear reduction in impact energy, despite still undergoing austempering. This deterioration is primarily attributed to the coarsening of the ausferritic microstructure at higher austempering temperatures, characterized by thicker ausferritic ferrite laths and lower carbon enrichment of retained austenite. Such microstructural changes reduce the mechanical stability of retained austenite and consequently decrease the matrix’s ability to absorb impact energy under dynamic loading. Moreover, depending on the transformation window, the onset of carbide precipitation may also contribute to the decline in impact toughness. 51 ,  52 – 53  Figure  9  further indicates that austempering duration also affects impact performance, especially at lower temperatures. When specimens processed at the same low austempering temperature are compared, the longer holding time leads to higher impact energy, suggesting that sufficient carbon partitioning into retained austenite is essential for improving toughness. A similar trend was reported in a previous study in which the specimen austempered at 350 °C for 60 minutes exhibited higher impact energy than the one austempered for 30 minutes. This behavior can be explained by insufficient stabilization of retained austenite during shorter holding periods, thereby increasing its susceptibility to strain-induced martensitic transformation under impact loading. 51 , 52  Accordingly, the impact response of SGCI is not controlled solely by the amount of retained austenite, but more importantly by its stability under dynamic loading conditions.

Figure  10  provides SEM fractographic evidence that helps explain the impact behavior of the austempered specimens. As shown in Figure  10 -(A), the fractured surface contains cleavage lines distributed over different regions. At the same time, Figure  10 -(B) reveals these fracture features in greater detail and also shows the presence of microvoids within the matrix. The coexistence of cleavage features and microvoids indicates that fracture occurred through a mixed mechanism involving both brittle and locally ductile contributions. In addition, the presence of well-defined graphite nodules and distinct dimples provides further insight into the fracture process. Although direct martensitic transformation is not expected during isothermal holding at 400 °C, localized strain-induced transformation of metastable retained austenite to martensite may occur during impact loading. Therefore, the reduced toughness observed in the high-temperature austempered specimens is more reasonably related to coarse ausferritic morphology and blocky retained austenite regions with reduced mechanical stability, rather than to martensite formation during heat treatment itself. Furthermore, manganese segregation in SGCI may influence the stability of retained austenite at elevated austempering temperatures, thereby promoting strain-induced martensitic transformation during impact loading and contributing to brittle fracture features. 37 , 54  Likewise, the reduced thermodynamic driving force for bainitic transformation at 400 °C and the altered carbon partitioning behavior may produce coarser ausferrite with larger regions of lower-stability austenite. 47 , 55 Figure 10 Impact failure surface of T1-300 austempered ductile cast iron.

sections.heading: Tribological Performance Approach
paragraphs: Figure  11  presents the average coefficient of friction (COF) values of the specimens under different applied loads. The graph clearly shows that the average COF increases with increasing wear load for all specimens, indicating stronger interfacial interaction under more severe contact conditions. In addition, specimens subjected to heat treatment, particularly austenitizing before austempering, exhibited higher friction coefficients than the as-cast samples. 56  Among the austempered specimens, increasing the austempering temperature 3 , 57 , 58  or extending the austempering time 59  generally led to lower COF values. This trend suggests that the reduction in hardness and the associated increase in ductility at higher austempering temperatures facilitate smoother sliding behavior, thereby lowering frictional resistance. Moreover, when these results are considered together with the hardness values in Figure  8 -(B), a clear relationship between hardness and coefficient of friction becomes evident. Figure  11  also highlights the tribological significance of graphite nodules in the SGCI matrix. In untreated specimens with relatively low hardness, graphite nodules tend to smear over the contact surface during wear and form a lubricating layer that helps reduce friction. However, in heat-treated specimens, especially after austempering or austenitizing, the stronger matrix and higher hardness limit the extent of graphite smearing. As a result, the lubricating effect of the graphite-derived surface film becomes less pronounced, particularly in the harder specimens produced at lower austempering temperatures. 8 , 9 , 56  This interpretation is also consistent with previous tribological studies showing that harder phases often lead to higher friction coefficients, and that increasing the applied load further intensifies this effect. 8 , 61  Similar observations have been reported in related experimental analyses. 2 , 62 Figure 11 Effect of heat treatment on the average COF of ductile cast iron.

Figure  12  presents the average specific wear-rate (SWR) values for the test specimens, along with their standard deviations. The results show that increasing austempering temperature and holding time leads to higher SWR values, indicating a progressive reduction in wear resistance. This trend is directly related to the loss of hardness and the coarsening of the ausferritic structure as austempering conditions become less favorable for microstructural refinement. The T1-300 specimen, which exhibited the highest hardness, showed the lowest SWR, whereas the high-temperature specimens displayed much larger wear losses. These findings confirm that wear resistance in the present SGCI system is primarily governed by matrix hardness and microstructural refinement, which together control the severity of material removal during abrasive sliding. Figure 12 Average SWR values of DCI materials subjected to different heat-treatment processes.

Figure  12  also gains further significance when the quantitative SWR values are interpreted alongside the SEM evidence in Figures  13 – 17 . The high-hardness T1-300 specimen exhibited the lowest SWR and mainly mild abrasive wear, characterized by shallow grooves and limited delamination. In contrast, the T1-400 and T2-400 specimens, which had lower hardness and higher SWR values, exhibited more severe abrasive plowing, deeper grooves, and more pronounced delamination. Intermediate conditions such as T1-350 and T2-350 exhibited mixed wear behavior, with both abrasive and adhesive contributions, consistent with their moderate hardness and wear resistance. Thus, the SWR results confirm that the dominant wear mechanisms evolve systematically with microstructure and hardness, rather than arising randomly from the test conditions alone. 60 , 63  Similarly, when specimens of comparable hardness are tested under different loads, those subjected to lower loads exhibit lower COF and SWR, indicating improved wear resistance under less severe contact conditions. Figure 13 SEM images of the worn surfaces of the DCI and A-900 specimens.

sections.heading: Characterization of Worn Surfaces
paragraphs: Figure  13  shows the SEM images of the worn surfaces of the as-cast DCI specimen and the A-900 specimen after abrasive wear testing. For the as-cast DCI specimen, pronounced plowing marks, valley-like grooves, nodular graphite structures, and severe plastic deformation are observed. Around the graphite nodules, the material exhibits a smeared appearance due to wear-induced plastic flow. In contrast, other regions reveal severe abrasive plowing, deep grooves, adhesive wear, random wear debris, microcracks, and material detachment. In addition, micron-scale pits and larger cavities caused by material removal are visible, and the applied load of 60 N appears to have intensified local stress concentrations and deformation. 58 , 63 ,  64 ,  65 – 66  These observations indicate that the as-cast DCI specimen suffered severe abrasive and adhesive wear, accompanied by delamination, consistent with its relatively low hardness and poor wear resistance. The A-900 specimen also exhibits prominent abrasive grooves, nodular structures, smearing around graphite nodules, detached particles, layered structures, deep furrows, cracks, delamination, and localized pits. Compared with the as-cast condition, the A-900 specimen still shows extensive surface damage, suggesting that austenitizing alone was insufficient to provide effective wear protection under the applied abrasive conditions.

Figure  14  presents the EDS characterization of the worn surface of the DCI specimen. The EDS results confirm the presence of an oxide layer formed during wear, demonstrating that oxidative wear contributed to the overall damage mechanism in addition to abrasive and adhesive wear. This finding is important because it shows that the wear process was not purely mechanical; rather, frictional heating and repeated surface contact also promoted tribochemical surface modification. When considered together with the SEM observations in Figure  13 , the EDS data support the interpretation that severe sliding contact in the low-hardness DCI specimen produced a complex wear regime involving plowing, adhesion, oxidation, and delamination. Figure 14 EDS characterization of the worn surface of the DCI specimen.

Figure  15  presents the SEM images of the worn surfaces of the T1-300 and T2-300 specimens after abrasive wear testing. The T1-300 specimen exhibits noticeable wear grooves, but these grooves are not associated with intense plowing. Smearing around the nodular regions, residual particle accumulation, localized cracks, pits, adhesive wear, flaking, and limited delamination are also observed. The T2-300 specimen likewise shows wear grooves, but the overall surface damage is relatively mild, with only partial grooves, pits, cracks, layered structures, and some delamination features. Figure 15 SEM images of the worn surfaces of T1-300 and T2-300 specimens.

Compared with the untreated and A-900 specimens, both T1-300 and T2-300 display significantly milder wear characteristics, confirming that the refined ausferritic structure formed at 300 °C provides much higher resistance to surface damage. In particular, the relatively shallow grooves and limited delamination are fully consistent with the lower SWR values measured for these specimens. 58 , 67 , 68

Figure  16  shows the worn surfaces of the T1-350 and T2-350 specimens. In the T1-350 specimen, pronounced wear grooves, localized wear debris around graphite nodules, adhesive wear regions, smearing, layered structures, pits, cracks, crack propagation zones, large debris pits, and delamination wear lines are observed. The T2-350 specimen exhibits visible wear grooves, slight debris around nodular regions, crack initiation, existing cracks, clustered pits, delamination traces, secondary plateaus, surface lifting, and adhesive wear zones. In addition, large-volume pit regions formed by delamination and spalling are clearly present. 66 ,  67 – 68  These features indicate that the specimens austempered at 350 °C exhibit an intermediate wear response, in which neither severe plowing nor fully mild wear dominates; instead, abrasive, adhesive, and delamination mechanisms act together in a balanced but still damaging manner. This mixed tribological response is consistent with the moderate hardness and SWR values measured at 350 °C. Figure 16 SEM images of the worn surfaces of T1-350 and T2-350 specimens.

Figure  17  presents the SEM images of the worn surfaces of the T1-400 and T2-400 specimens. The T1-400 specimen shows clearly defined wear tracks, nodular graphite regions, partial wear debris accumulation, crack initiation, pits, delamination, material detachment, flaking, adhesive wear, and areas where a translucent layer formed over graphite nodules as a result of plastic deformation and the lubricating action of graphite. 62 , 68  The T2-400 specimen exhibits well-defined wear tracks, deep grooved valleys, pronounced plastic deformation around graphite nodules, crack-induced pits and splits, severe delamination, peeling, material spalling, and secondary surface layers associated with graphite-assisted lubrication. 56 , 68  Although graphite still provides some local lubricating effect in these high-temperature specimens, it is clearly insufficient to compensate for the reduced matrix hardness and the coarser microstructure. Therefore, the dominant wear features in both T1-400 and T2-400 are much more severe than those observed in the 300 °C specimens, which explains their higher SWR values and poorer tribological performance. Figure 17 SEM images of the worn surfaces of T1-400 and T2-400 specimens.

sections.heading: Comparative Evaluation with Literature and Standards
paragraphs: Table  6  compares the present results with previously reported literature data and the relevant ASTM quality standards. The comparison shows that several of the produced specimens not only satisfy the ASTM requirements but also approach or exceed the upper ranges reported in some literature studies for tensile strength and hardness. In particular, the T1-300 specimen exhibited a UTS of 1344.8 ± 32.97 MPa and a hardness of 52.92 ± 1.64 HRC, while still maintaining measurable ductility. Likewise, T2-300 and T1-350 also provided competitive combinations of strength and elongation. These results indicate that the selected austempering schedules, especially at low temperature and short duration, were highly effective in producing favorable strength–ductility–wear property balances in the present Si–Mo ferritic ductile iron system. Table  6  also shows that direct comparison with literature data must be approached carefully. Although the present study produced highly competitive tensile strength, elongation, hardness, and COF values, the testing conditions used in previous studies vary considerably in terms of austempering temperature, holding time, applied load, sliding speed, abrasive medium, and test configuration. 48 , 60 , 69  Therefore, the present results should be interpreted as demonstrating a favorable and competitive property combination under comparable conditions, rather than as universal superiority over all previously published data. In this context, it is more scientifically accurate to conclude that a short-duration, low-temperature austempering schedule (300 °C for 30 min) in Si–Mo ferritic ductile iron processed via SSF provides a particularly advantageous balance of high tensile strength, high hardness, and improved wear resistance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The mechanical and tribological performance of SGCI specimens subjected to different austempering parameters was systematically evaluated through tensile, hardness, impact, and wear tests. The results revealed that the specimen austempered at 300 °C for 30 minutes (T1-300) exhibited the highest tensile strength (1344.8 MPa ±32.97 MPa) and hardness (52.92 HRC ±1.64 HRC). In contrast, the highest impact toughness (54.70 J ±4.443) was achieved in the specimen austempered at 300 °C for 90 minutes (T2-300). In contrast, as-cast samples exhibited the lowest strength and hardness, while austenitized specimens showed the lowest impact toughness. From a tribological perspective, the T1-300 samples exhibited the most favorable wear resistance with the lowest specific wear rates, whereas the as-cast specimens displayed inferior wear performance.

Beyond these numerical findings, the results clearly demonstrate a strong process–microstructure–property relationship governed by austempering temperature and holding time. Lower austempering temperatures (300 °C) promote the formation of a refined ausferritic microstructure comprising fine acicular ferrite and carbon-enriched retained austenite, thereby contributing to superior strength and wear resistance. In contrast, higher austempering temperatures (350–400 °C) result in coarser ausferritic structures and increased amounts of blocky retained austenite, leading to improved ductility but reduced strength and wear resistance.

The influence of austempering duration further highlights that shorter holding times (30 min) favor higher strength and hardness due to finer microstructural features. In contrast, longer holding times (90 min) enhance impact toughness by promoting carbon partitioning and stabilizing retained austenite. Therefore, the T1-300 condition should be interpreted as providing an optimal balance of strength–wear resistance rather than the best overall performance, since maximum toughness was obtained under a different condition (T2-300). Microstructural observations also indicate that graphite morphology remains largely unaffected by austempering. In contrast, matrix evolution, particularly the distribution, morphology, and stability of retained austenite, plays a dominant role in determining mechanical and tribological responses. These findings indicate that a single microstructural parameter does not govern the mechanical response. Still, the combined effects of ausferritic refinement retained austenite stability and the morphological distribution of retained austenite within the matrix.

The increase in retained austenite fraction at higher temperatures, accompanied by reduced carbon enrichment, further supports the transition from stable film-like austenite to less stable blocky morphologies. According to the comparison presented in Table  6 , the mechanical properties obtained in this study are comparable to relevant ASTM classifications; however, claims of standard compliance or superiority should be interpreted with caution, as a complete classification framework that includes all required parameters has not yet been fully established.

Finally, several methodological limitations should be acknowledged. Phase quantification based on XRD analysis is inherently uncertain due to incomplete peak deconvolution, and the presence of martensite cannot be conclusively confirmed or excluded. In addition, although no clear microstructural evidence of martensite formation was observed in SEM and XRD analyses, its localized presence cannot be entirely ruled out. It may contribute to the high strength observed under certain conditions. Additionally, the wear mechanism analysis is primarily based on qualitative SEM observations, which may limit quantitative interpretation. These limitations should be considered when evaluating the results, and future studies incorporating advanced phase characterization and quantitative wear analysis are recommended. Overall, this study establishes a comprehensive framework that links austempering parameters to microstructural evolution and the resulting mechanical–tribological performance, demonstrating that careful control of transformation conditions enables tailoring of the balance between strength, toughness, and wear resistance in Si–Mo alloyed ductile iron systems.
